title: Building Automation APIs and Services with FastAPI
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Building Automation APIs and Services with FastAPI ##### When the no-code tool becomes the bottleneck A team's invoice pipeline ran in n8n, and 90% of it was a good fit — triggers, routing, notifications, CRM writes. But one node had grown into 300 lines of JavaScript that parsed a bank statement format, reconciled it against ledger entries, and computed allocations. That node could not be unit tested. It could not be code-reviewed meaningfully. It had no type checking. Two engineers had introduced conflicting edits because the "diff" was two screenshots. And it ran inside a workflow execution, so a slow parse blocked a worker slot. The fix was not migrating away from n8n. It was extracting that logic into a **FastAPI service** with tests and types, and having n8n call it over HTTP. The workflow kept the orchestration it was good at; the service took the computation it was good at. Knowing when — and how — to build a small API service is what removes the ceiling from an automation practice. ##### Why FastAPI FastAPI combines four things that matter for this use case: **Pydantic-based validation** (the boundary discipline from yesterday, enforced by the framework), **automatic OpenAPI documentation** generated from your type hints, **async support** for high-concurrency I/O, and **dependency injection** for clean auth and resource management. The automatic documentation deserves emphasis. Because your request and response models *are* Python types, FastAPI derives the OpenAPI schema from them — so `/docs` always matches the code. Documentation that cannot drift is a genuinely different proposition from documentation you maintain. ##### A minimal, correct service ```python from datetime import datetime from decimal import Decimal from typing import Annotated, Literal from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends, Header, HTTPException, Request, status from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field app = FastAPI( title="Automation Services", version="1.0.0", description="Internal endpoints used by n8n and Make workflows.", ) class LineItem(BaseModel): sku: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1, max_length=32)] quantity: Annotated[int, Field(gt=0, le=1000)] unit_price: Annotated[Decimal, Field(ge=0, decimal_places=2)] class ReconcileRequest(BaseModel): statement_id: str currency: Literal["INR", "USD"] = "INR" items: Annotated[list[LineItem], Field(min_length=1)] notify: EmailStr | None = None class ReconcileResponse(BaseModel): statement_id: str matched: int unmatched: int total: Decimal processed_at: datetime @app.post( "/v1/reconcile", response_model=ReconcileResponse, status_code=status.HTTP_200_OK, summary="Reconcile statement lines against the ledger", tags=["finance"], ) async def reconcile(payload: ReconcileRequest) -> ReconcileResponse: result = await run_reconciliation(payload) # testable pure-ish logic return ReconcileResponse(**result) ``` Everything about validation is free here. A request with `quantity: 0`, a malformed email, or a missing `statement_id` never reaches your function — FastAPI returns a `422` with a structured error naming the exact field and constraint. That is the assignment's first question in practice: **the models are simultaneously the validator, the serializer, and the documentation.** ##### Authentication with dependency injection Dependencies are FastAPI's mechanism for shared, testable, composable pre-request logic. ```python import hmac, secrets from fastapi import Security from fastapi.security import APIKeyHeader api_key_header = APIKeyHeader(name="X-API-Key", auto_error=False) async def require_api_key(key: str | None = Security(api_key_header)) -> str: """Validate the caller's API key in constant time.""" if not key: raise HTTPException(401, "missing X-API-Key header") for name, valid in settings.api_keys.items(): # supports rotation if hmac.compare_digest(key, valid.get_secret_value()): return name raise HTTPException(403, "invalid API key") # Applied per-route... @app.post("/v1/reconcile", dependencies=[Depends(require_api_key)]) async def reconcile(payload: ReconcileRequest) -> ReconcileResponse: ... # ...or to a whole router from fastapi import APIRouter internal = APIRouter(prefix="/v1", dependencies=[Depends(require_api_key)]) ``` Three benefits over inline checks. The dependency is **declared**, so it appears in the OpenAPI schema and the `/docs` page shows a lock icon. It is **testable in isolation**. And it is **overridable in tests** via `app.dependency_overrides[require_api_key] = lambda: "test-client"`, which means your test suite does not need real credentials. Dependencies also handle resource lifecycle: ```python async def get_db() -> AsyncIterator[AsyncSession]: async with SessionLocal() as session: yield session # cleanup guaranteed after response ``` ##### A webhook receiver done properly This is the highest-value endpoint an automation engineer builds, and it combines the signature verification and fast-ack discipline from earlier work. ```python import hashlib, hmac, json, time from fastapi import BackgroundTasks def verify(raw: bytes, header: str, secret: str, tolerance: int = 300) -> None: try: parts = dict(p.split("=", 1) for p in header.split(",")) ts, provided = parts["t"], parts["v1"] except (ValueError, KeyError): raise HTTPException(401, "malformed signature") if abs(time.time() - int(ts)) > tolerance: raise HTTPException(401, "timestamp outside tolerance") # replay guard expected = hmac.new(secret.encode(), f"{ts}.".encode() + raw, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest() if not hmac.compare_digest(expected, provided): raise HTTPException(401, "signature mismatch") @app.post("/webhooks/payments", status_code=status.HTTP_202_ACCEPTED) async def payments_webhook( request: Request, background: BackgroundTasks, signature: Annotated[str, Header(alias="X-Signature")] = "", db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db), ) -> dict[str, str]: raw = await request.body() # raw bytes BEFORE parsing verify(raw, signature, settings.webhook_secret.get_secret_value()) event = json.loads(raw) # Durable + idempotent: the PK makes a duplicate insert a no-op inserted = await db.execute( insert(WebhookEvent) .values(event_id=event["id"], event_type=event["type"], payload=raw.decode()) .on_conflict_do_nothing(index_elements=["event_id"]) .returning(WebhookEvent.event_id) ) await db.commit() if inserted.scalar_one_or_none() is None: return {"status": "duplicate"} # already have it, still 202 background.add_task(process_payment_event, event["id"]) return {"status": "accepted"} ``` Note the ordering — verify, parse, **persist**, then schedule — and that the endpoint returns in milliseconds regardless of how slow processing is. A caveat on `BackgroundTasks`: it runs **in the same process after the response is sent**. That is perfect for quick follow-ups, and inadequate for anything long or important, because a restart loses it. For real work, enqueue to Celery/RQ instead. The persist-first pattern above means even a lost background task is recoverable by a sweeper. ##### Error handling and status codes Return the status code that describes what happened, and give the caller something actionable: ```python from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse class DomainError(Exception): def __init__(self, code: str, message: str, status_code: int = 400): self.code, self.message, self.status_code = code, message, status_code @app.exception_handler(DomainError) async def domain_error_handler(request: Request, exc: DomainError) -> JSONResponse: log.warning("domain_error", code=exc.code, path=request.url.path) return JSONResponse( status_code=exc.status_code, content={"error": {"code": exc.code, "message": exc.message, "request_id": request.state.request_id}}, ) ``` | Situation | Code | |---|---| | Success with body | `200` | | Created a resource | `201` | | Accepted for async processing | `202` | | Validation failure | `422` (FastAPI's default) | | Missing/invalid credential | `401` | | Valid credential, not permitted | `403` | | Unknown resource | `404` | | Idempotency/state conflict | `409` | | Rate limited | `429` + `Retry-After` | | Unexpected server fault | `500` | The consuming workflow depends on these being right: your n8n HTTP node's retry logic keys off 5xx versus 4xx exactly as described in earlier days. Add a **request ID middleware** so every log line and error response carries a correlation ID: ```python @app.middleware("http") async def add_request_id(request: Request, call_next): rid = request.headers.get("X-Request-ID", secrets.token_hex(8)) request.state.request_id = rid structlog.contextvars.bind_contextvars(request_id=rid, path=request.url.path) response = await call_next(request) response.headers["X-Request-ID"] = rid return response ``` ##### Testing ```python import pytest from fastapi.testclient import TestClient @pytest.fixture def client(): app.dependency_overrides[require_api_key] = lambda: "test-client" with TestClient(app) as c: yield c app.dependency_overrides.clear() def test_reconcile_rejects_zero_quantity(client): r = client.post("/v1/reconcile", json={ "statement_id": "ST-1", "items": [{"sku": "A", "quantity": 0, "unit_price": "10.00"}], }) assert r.status_code == 422 assert r.json()["detail"][0]["loc"] == ["body", "items", 0, "quantity"] def test_webhook_rejects_bad_signature(client): r = client.post("/webhooks/payments", content=b'{"id":"e1"}', headers={"X-Signature": "t=1,v1=deadbeef"}) assert r.status_code == 401 ``` Because validation is declarative, most of your tests target *behaviour* rather than input checking — the framework has already covered the latter. ##### Where a service beats no-code ```mermaid flowchart LR T[Trigger: webhook] --> N[n8n workflow] N -->|orchestrates| A[Slack notify] N -->|orchestrates| B[CRM update] N -->|HTTP POST| S[FastAPI service
typed · tested · versioned] S --> P[(Postgres)] S -->|enqueue| Q[(Celery/Redis)] Q --> W[Workers] S -->|202 fast| N ``` Two scenarios where the custom service is the right call, as the assignment asks: **1. Complex, testable domain logic.** The bank-statement reconciliation from the opening. Anything requiring unit tests, a real library, type checking, or code review by more than one person belongs in a repository — not in a text box inside a workflow node. The workflow still orchestrates; the service computes. **2. High-volume or latency-sensitive ingestion.** A webhook endpoint receiving thousands of events an hour, needing signature verification, deduplication and sub-50 ms acknowledgment, will be both cheaper and faster as a FastAPI service than as billable workflow executions. It also gives you a durable store and a queue that the no-code platform's execution model does not. Two more worth mentioning: **reusable internal APIs** consumed by several workflows and several tools, and **anything requiring precise control** over connection pooling, streaming, or protocols the platform does not support. The composition principle holds throughout: **use the workflow tool for orchestration and integration breadth; use a service for computation, ingestion and anything that needs software engineering discipline.** ##### Common pitfalls - **Blocking calls in `async def`** — `requests`, `time.sleep`, sync database drivers freeze the event loop. Use async clients or `def` (FastAPI runs sync handlers in a threadpool). - **Parsing the body before verifying** a webhook signature. - **Relying on `BackgroundTasks`** for durable work. - **Returning 500 for validation problems**, causing callers to retry pointlessly. - **No `response_model`**, leaking internal fields and losing documentation. - **Auth checks inline** rather than as dependencies — untestable and undocumented. - **Exposing `/docs` publicly** on an internal service; disable or protect it in production. - **No request ID**, making cross-system debugging guesswork. - **Unversioned paths** — start with `/v1/` before you need it. - **Missing rate limiting**, letting one misconfigured workflow saturate the service. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: build a FastAPI service with a **webhook endpoint** that validates the payload via a **Pydantic model**, **verifies a signature**, **returns 200/202 quickly**, and **schedules processing as a background task**, with automatic OpenAPI docs. Then open `/docs` and exercise the endpoint from the browser — seeing your models rendered as an interactive spec is the moment the "documentation cannot drift" claim becomes concrete. The mini project is an **internal automation API**: multiple endpoints with Pydantic validation, **API-key auth via dependencies**, a webhook receiver that **enqueues to a task queue**, error handling with proper status codes, auto docs, and a **test suite**. Then wire it into an n8n or Make workflow via an HTTP node — the round trip from workflow to service and back is the architecture this whole day is building toward. For the assignment, explain **how FastAPI plus Pydantic provide automatic validation and documentation** — one type definition serving as validator, serializer and OpenAPI schema — and describe **two automation scenarios where a custom service beats no-code alone**. Argue from engineering properties: testability, reviewability, type safety, cost per execution, and latency. ##### Key takeaways - FastAPI turns Pydantic models into request validation, response serialization and always-accurate OpenAPI docs from a single type definition. - Use dependency injection for authentication and resource lifecycle — declared, documented, testable, and overridable in tests. - Webhook receivers should verify the raw body's signature with a timestamp tolerance, persist idempotently, then return 202 fast and process elsewhere. - Return status codes that mean something: 422 for validation, 401/403 for auth, 409 for conflicts, 429 with `Retry-After` — consuming workflows key their retry logic off them. - Build a service when logic needs tests, types and review, or when ingestion volume and latency demand it; keep the workflow tool for orchestration and integration breadth.
